title: Brand strategy
heading: Brand strategy — Okwe Knowledge
html:
Brand strategy — Okwe Knowledge

Everything here is a design decision written in words. It exists so that a small team can make consistent choices without asking anyone.

What Okwe Knowledge is

The intelligence, education and capability platform of the Okwe ecosystem. At launch it is one thing only: a publisher that researches how trade, logistics and enterprise actually work, and teaches it. Academy, research, community, IP and innovation are capabilities we earn, not departments we announce.

Launch loop: Question → Research → Content → Audience → Feedback → Product → Course → Knowledge.

The fundamental belief

Knowledge should increase people's ability to participate productively in the real economy. If a piece does not increase somebody's capability, it is not ours to publish.

Positioning statement

For operators in African trade, logistics and enterprise who are tired of choosing between motivational content and inaccessible academic work, Okwe Knowledge explains how the real economy actually works — decomposed, sourced, and immediately usable. Unlike creator-led business accounts, we show our method; unlike research institutions, we write for the person doing the work this week.

Brand essence

Understanding, made usable.

Brand promise

We will explain something you can use this week, and we will show you where we got it.

Mission / vision

  • Mission. Turn evidence and experience into capability, one published piece at a time.
  • Vision. A knowledge institution whose research is trusted enough that businesses, and eventually the wider Okwe ecosystem, plan around it.

Values

  1. Decompose. A number you cannot break down is a number you do not understand.
  2. Show the method. How we know is part of what we know.
  3. Say what you don't know. The honesty line is a feature, not a weakness.
  4. Simple language, sophisticated thinking. Never the reverse.
  5. Field over theory. Where possible, measure something real.
  6. Publish less, better. One piece that changes a decision beats five that get seen.

Archetype — Sage · Builder · Explorer

The brief's instinct is right, but the weighting matters:

  • Sage (lead, ~55%). The reason to follow: we explain and we are accurate. Sets the editorial voice, the serif headline, the source note, the calm palette.
  • Builder (~30%). The reason to trust: we describe things that work, in the order they work. Sets the framework format, numbered decomposition, the Okwe Principle, the squared-off geometry and hairline grid.
  • Explorer (~15%). The reason to keep reading: we go and look. Sets Field Notes, first-person plural reporting, photography of real operations, the honesty line.

What we rejected: Teacher as lead (it flattens into course-selling before we have earned an audience) and Strategist as lead (it pulls the brand toward consulting-speak, the one voice we cannot afford).

Effects of this weighting:

  • Visual: editorial and institutional, not tech-startup. Serif headlines (Sage), rule-and-grid structure (Builder), documentary photography (Explorer).
  • Voice: explanatory first, prescriptive second, never exhortatory.
  • Content: explainers and frameworks are the core; field notes are the differentiator; commentary is rationed.
  • Product: we teach only what we have already published and been questioned about.

Audience

Primary (launch): operators in African trade and logistics — first-time and small importers, distributors, procurement and logistics staff, and the founders who do all three jobs. Lagos first, then Nairobi, Accra, Johannesburg.

Secondary: professionals abroad who deal with African markets — sourcing managers, freight partners, development and finance analysts.

Tertiary (later): institutions who eventually buy training and research.

We start narrow deliberately: first-time and small importers pricing goods. That audience has an expensive, repeated, answerable problem.

Messaging pillars

  1. How it actually works. Mechanics over abstractions.
  2. Decompose the number. Cost, time and risk broken into lines you can act on.
  3. Evidence you can check. Sources, method, and what we could not establish.
  4. Capability, not motivation. The measure of a piece is what you can now do.
  5. Built for the real economy. Trade, movement and enterprise — the physical economy, not the discourse about it.

Differentiation — the four questions answered

  • Why follow us instead of another business account? Because we publish decompositions and measurements, with sources, and we say when we are uncertain.
  • Why buy an Okwe course? Because it only exists after the free work proved the demand and the teaching was already questioned in public.
  • Why trust Okwe research? Because the method note and the limits are published alongside the finding.
  • Why join the wider ecosystem later? Because the knowledge arm will have accumulated something no one else has: measured, structured detail about how these markets actually operate.

Visual territory

Chosen: the working document of the real economy. Not an editorial or ed-tech look but a notation system — chalk mineral ground, cyanotype blueprint ink, sulphur marking ink, verdigris for systems, and four recurring devices that carry information rather than decorate it: the call number, the tally, the manifest diagram and the margin note. Type is Archivo at expanded width against Martian Mono at narrow width, with Literata for reading. The full argument, the five territories tested and the palette and typography candidates are in visual-thesis.md.

Rejected territories, and why:

  • Optimistic ed-tech (rounded cards, bright gradients, illustration) — reads as a course funnel; borrows credibility it hasn't earned.
  • Consulting corporate (navy, glass towers, stock photography) — sounds like the jargon we banned.
  • Pan-African heritage (green/gold, kente pattern, adinkra) — decorative shortcut; ties the brand to a decoration instead of an idea.
  • Brutalist data-terminal (all mono, black/green, grid) — distinctive but cold, and unreadable in a carousel at phone size.

The territory is grounded through the name and the material culture of the work: okwe is a sowing-and-reaping board game where seeds are counted, moved and compounded — which is where the tally comes from — and the economy Okwe writes about runs on manifests, waybills, tally books and stamps, which is where the notation comes from. Grounded in subject matter and photography, never in pattern.

Editorial philosophy

Trust → usefulness → authority → audience → revenue. In that order, and never reordered for a view count. We do not publish to a schedule we cannot research to.

What this brand is not

Not a motivational page, not a guru, not a news outlet, not a content farm, not an academic journal, not a personality. If a piece would work with a stock quote and a face on it, it is not ours.

title: Voice & writing
heading: Voice, writing and editorial standards
html:
Voice, writing and editorial standards

The voice in one line

Simple language, sophisticated thinking. We explain complicated things plainly, and we never pretend to know more than we do.

Instead of: "Organizations must leverage cross-functional synergies to optimize strategic resource allocation." Write: "A group becomes valuable when its businesses can share capabilities without losing operational independence."

Voice attributes and how they show up

AttributeIn practice
ClearOne idea per paragraph. Define a term the first time you use it.
IntelligentNever dumb the subject down; simplify the sentence instead.
PracticalEvery piece ends where the reader can act.
Evidence-orientedFact, interpretation and opinion are labelled, not blended.
CuriousReal questions, asked in public, including ones we haven't answered.
InstitutionalThink in systems, incentives, capabilities and outcomes.
HumanContractions are fine. Bureaucratic constructions are not.
Confident but humbleStrong claims, stated limits.

Person and tone

  • We for the institution: "we tracked two shipments", "we could not establish".
  • You for the reader: "your margin dies after the invoice".
  • Never I on brand channels; individual authorship goes in the byline, not the voice.
  • Sentence case everywhere except mono labels (THE TRADE DESK) and the wordmark.
  • No emoji. No exclamation marks. No rhetorical "Let that sink in."

Writing rules

Sentences. Average 14–18 words. One idea each. Vary length; use a short sentence to land a point. Paragraphs. 1–4 sentences on web, 1–2 on social. Never a wall. Vocabulary. Plain words for common things; technical terms only where precision is required — then defined once, in six words or fewer. Banned constructions. leverage, synergy, utilise, unlock, empower, game-changer, revolutionary, "in today's fast-paced world", "the next generation of". Numbers. Always attributed. Round only when rounding does not change the decision. State the sample: "two shipments" beats "our research shows". Examples. Concrete and local. A named route beats "international markets". Analogies. One per piece, and only if it survives scrutiny. Claims. Every claim gets a class: fact (sourced), interpretation (our reading), opinion (our view), unknown (stated). Use the Badge tones. Uncertainty. Write it: "We do not know whether this holds outside this route." Disagreement. Argue with the position, name it fairly, never the person. Controversy. Only where we have evidence and a reason to be useful. No political alignment. Corrections. Correct in place, mark the change, keep the original claim visible: Corrected 20 Aug 2026 — original said 63%; recalculated to 61% after including terminal handling.

Headlines and hooks

Headline rules: the subject, plainly, in ≤62 characters. Searchable, not clickbait.

  • Good: "What landed cost actually includes"
  • Good: "Why your container waits at the port"
  • Bad: "The shocking truth about importing"
  • Bad: "5 secrets nobody tells you about freight"

Hook rules (first line of any post or video): state the mistake, the number, or the question. Never tease.

  • "Most importers price from the invoice. The invoice is the smallest part of the number."
  • "We timed two containers from berth to warehouse. Customs was not the delay."

Calls to action

One per asset, plain, no urgency theatre.

  • "Read the full piece — okweknowledge.com"
  • "The framework is in the brief. One email a week."
  • Never: "Link in bio!! 🔥", "Don't miss out", "Tag someone who needs this".

Structural templates

Explainer. Hook → what it is → how it works → why it matters → one takeaway. Framework. Problem → numbered steps (max 5) → Okwe Principle. Case file. Situation → decision → result → lesson. Label hypothetical cases as hypothetical. Myth. What people say → why it seems right → what is actually true → what to do instead. Numbers. The figure → how we measured it → what it does not prove. Field note. Where we were → what we saw → what we measured → what surprised us → what we still cannot explain. Definition. Term → plain definition → what it is not → why the confusion is expensive.

Content quality framework

Score every proposed piece 0–5 on ten criteria: usefulness, accuracy, originality, clarity, relevance, evidence, practical application, audience fit, longevity, brand fit.

  • Publishing threshold: 35/50, with no single score below 3.
  • Accuracy or evidence below 3 is a hard stop, whatever the total.
  • Below threshold: it becomes research, not a post.
  • The editor records the score in the calendar. A piece nobody scored is a piece nobody owns.

Trust mechanisms (non-negotiable)

  1. Sources listed, with dates.
  2. Method note on anything quantitative.
  3. "What we don't know" on anything researched.
  4. Date stamp on every asset; update stamps on revision.
  5. Named author on long-form.
  6. Corrections policy published and linked.
  7. Hypotheticals labelled: "Illustrative example — not a measured figure."

title: Social playbook
heading: Social playbook
html:
Social playbook

Principle: social media is distribution; the website and the email list are infrastructure. Every platform's job ends with somebody on okweknowledge.com or the Weekly Brief.

Platform tiers

Tier 1 — where we actually build (launch).

PlatformRoleCadence at launch
XIdeas, frameworks, decompositions, questions, threads on live research5 posts + 1 thread / week
LinkedInProfessional analysis, document posts, case files, hiring credibility3 posts + 1 document / week
YouTubeThe deep asset: one explainer that everything else is cut from1 video / 2 weeks

Why: X and LinkedIn are text-first, so a two-person team can produce them from the research itself. YouTube is where a 14-minute explanation is welcome and where search compounds for years.

Tier 2 — repurposing surfaces.

PlatformRoleCadence
InstagramCarousels, definitions, statistic cards3 / week, all derived
TikTok / Reels / ShortsOne-concept explainers cut from the video3 / week, all derived

Why Tier 2: high production cost per unit of trust, and neither converts to an owned audience as directly. They earn Tier 1 status only when a carousel or short reliably drives brief signups.

Tier 3 — presence, not effort. Facebook and Threads: mirror the strongest Tier 1 post, claim the handles, answer comments. No original production.

Deprioritised — Twitch. Live formats need an audience that already turns up on a schedule. Revisit only when (a) the Weekly Brief passes ~2,000 subscribers and (b) we are already running live workshops that people pay for. A recorded workshop on YouTube does the same job with less risk.

Platform writing rules

X. Ideas first, no preamble. One insight per post. Threads only when the complexity requires it — 5–9 posts, numbered, first post standalone, last post the source note. Reply to real questions; do not argue with bad faith. LinkedIn. Professional but human. Lead with the finding, then the reasoning. 3–6 short paragraphs. Document posts carry the carousel PDF. No "agree?" bait. Instagram. Cover earns the swipe; slides 2–5 teach; last slide is the CTA. Caption repeats the takeaway in two sentences plus the source line. TikTok / Shorts. Hook in the first 2 seconds — the mistake or the number. One concept, 45–90 seconds. Subtitles always (mono, bottom third, inside the safe zone). End card, not a hard sell. YouTube. Searchable title, honest thumbnail, chapters, sources in the description. Structure: question → why it matters → mechanics → worked example → what we don't know. Facebook / Threads. Same substance, plainer framing, links welcome.

Series architecture (start with four)

SeriesPurposeFormatFrequency
The Trade DeskImport, export, sourcing, pricing mechanicsExplainer + frameworkWeekly
The Logistics DeskFreight, ports, warehousing, movementExplainer + case fileFortnightly
Field NotesWhat we saw and measured in the real economyReportMonthly
NumbersOne measured figure, honestly caveatedData cardWeekly (short)

Held back until the first four are consistent: Business Anatomy, How It Works, Case File, Okwe Explains. Four series is a rhythm; twelve is a backlog.

Repurposing — the atomisation framework

One research project → one core asset → many expressions. Never the same post everywhere.

RESEARCH: "How international sourcing works"
   │
   ├── YouTube explainer (14 min)            ← the core asset
   ├── Website article + source note          ← the owned home
   ├── X thread (the decomposition)           ← the argument
   ├── LinkedIn document post (the framework) ← the professional proof
   ├── Instagram carousel (6 slides)          ← the visual teaching
   ├── 3 short-form clips (one concept each)  ← discovery
   ├── Statistic card (one measured number)   ← shareable evidence
   ├── Weekly Brief issue                     ← the owned audience
   └── Workshop module → course module        ← the product path

Rule: each expression must be useful on its own. If it only makes sense as a trailer for the video, it is not an asset.

Community management

  • Answer questions that a future piece could be built from; log them in the question register.
  • Thank corrections publicly and fix the asset.
  • Do not debate politics, do not dunk, do not engagement-farm.
  • Response window: 24 hours on Tier 1, best effort elsewhere.

Search and hashtags

  • X: no hashtags. Plain keywords in the sentence.
  • LinkedIn: 3 maximum, topical (#trade #logistics #procurement).
  • Instagram: 5–8, specific and unbranded, plus #okweknowledge.
  • YouTube: keywords in the title and first description line; no keyword stuffing.

Metrics (and what we ignore)

LayerMeasuresDecision it informs
Attentionimpressions, reach, viewswhich topics get discovered
Engagementsaves, shares, comments, watch timewhich teaching actually landed
Audiencefollowers, brief subscribers, returning visitorswhether distribution is becoming infrastructure
Learningworkshop attendance, completion, feedbackwhether we can teach it
Commercialleads, conversions, revenue, CACwhether a product is viable
Strategicrepeated questions, emerging topicswhat to research and teach next

The two numbers that govern the strategy: saves/shares per piece (usefulness) and brief subscribers per week (infrastructure). Follower count is reported, never optimised.

Experimentation

One experiment per month, one variable, written down before it runs: hypothesis, metric, duration, decision rule. Kill or adopt at the end. No permanent pilots.

title: Content playbook
heading: Content playbook — how an idea becomes an Okwe piece
html:
Content playbook — how an idea becomes an Okwe piece

The editorial operating system

IDEA → QUESTION → RESEARCH → OUTLINE → DRAFT → FACT CHECK → EDIT
     → DESIGN → PUBLISH → DISTRIBUTE → MEASURE → LEARN → UPDATE

Each stage has an owner, an artefact and an exit condition.

StageArtefactExit condition
IdeaOne line in the question registerIt is phrased as a question somebody actually asked
QuestionThe precise question, plus who has itYou can say what changes for the reader if it is answered
ResearchNotes with sources, at least one primary contact or measurementYou can decompose the answer into parts
OutlineStructure from the format templatesEvery section has a purpose
DraftProse in the house voiceNo unsupported claims remain
Fact checkClaim-by-claim pass; each labelled fact / interpretation / opinion / unknownEvery number has a source and a method
EditQuality score 0–5 × 10 criteria≥35/50, nothing below 3
DesignAssets built in the Post Editor from templatesSafe zones respected, series label present, source line present
PublishArticle live with source note and date stampOwned home exists before distribution
DistributePlatform assets per the atomisation frameworkEach expression useful alone
MeasureWeekly numbers in the calendarSaves/shares and brief signups recorded
LearnOne sentence on what to do differentlyWritten down, not remembered
UpdateRevision with a change noteOriginal claim still visible

The question register

The most valuable file in the company. Every question from a comment, DM, workshop or conversation goes in with: the question, where it came from, the date, how many times it has appeared, and whether we can answer it with evidence. Research priority = frequency × cost of getting it wrong.

Batching (two-person team)

DayWork
MondayResearch + question register review
TuesdayWriting (article + brief)
WednesdayDesign + record
ThursdayPublish article + brief; post Tier 1
FridayCut derivatives, schedule Tier 2, record numbers

Publishing rhythms — pick the one the team can actually sustain:

  • Minimum viable: 1 article, 1 brief, 5 X posts, 2 LinkedIn posts, 1 carousel per week. One video per month.
  • Sustainable growth (target by month 3): the above plus a fortnightly video and 3 shorts per week.
  • Scaled (needs a third person: a designer/editor): 2 articles, weekly video, daily Tier 1, 5 shorts per week.

Never raise the rhythm before the quality scores hold for four consecutive weeks.

Content pillars at launch (three, not ten)

  1. Trade — sourcing, import mechanics, pricing, documentation. ~50% of output.
  2. Logistics — freight, ports, warehousing, delivery. ~30%.
  3. Business capability — the operating decisions that use the first two: pricing, credit, margin, supplier management. ~20%.

Economics, systems thinking, tools and research are treatments, not pillars, until the audience asks for them by name.

Content → product

Repeated question → content cluster (3–5 pieces) → audience demand
   → free resource (checklist / calculator) → paid workshop
   → course → professional programme → B2B training → research product

Product validation score (0–3 each; build at ≥12/18, and never below 2 on willingness to pay): question frequency · sustained engagement · resource downloads · explicit requests · willingness to pay (pre-sale or waitlist) · demonstrable learner outcome.

A topic becomes a workshop only after: 3+ published pieces, 30+ related questions, and a stated outcome we can test in three hours.

Course discovery

Each month, rank the question register by frequency, then filter: Can we answer it with evidence? Is it expensive to get wrong? Can a learner demonstrate the new capability the same week? Top item becomes the next free resource; the one after it becomes the next workshop. Audience question → frequency → importance → willingness to pay → learning outcome → product test.

30-day launch plan

WeekWork
1 — FoundationClaim handles; set profiles from the Social Kit; publish "What we publish and how" plus the corrections policy; stand up the site and the brief; open the question register.
2 — ProofPublish the flagship piece (landed cost) with full source note; 5 X posts + 1 thread; 2 LinkedIn posts; first carousel; first Numbers card.
3 — DepthPublish piece two (why containers wait) and the first Field Note; first YouTube explainer; free resource: the landed-cost checklist (email-gated); begin logging questions.
4 — Read and adjustPublish piece three; review scores and metrics; write the first learning note; announce the first workshop only if the validation score clears 12.

Success at day 30 is not followers. It is: 3 published pieces at ≥35/50, one resource, a question register with 30+ entries, and a functioning weekly rhythm.

90-day framework

WeeksThemeObjectiveProduct signal to watch
1–4Landed cost and pricingProve the format and the trust systemChecklist downloads
5–8Movement: ports, clearing, delayShow field measurement as our edgeRepeated questions about documentation
9–12Supplier and margin decisionsConnect trade to business capabilityWaitlist for the pricing workshop

Each week: one research question, one core asset, one derivative set, one measurement note. At week 12, decide the first paid product from evidence — not from ambition.

Governance

  • Nothing publishes without a scored edit. The editor is a role, not a person's mood.
  • Design consistency: assets are made in the Post Editor from named templates; ad-hoc canvases are not published.
  • Template changes are proposals, reviewed once a month, then versioned (-02).
  • Naming: OKW-[DOMAIN]-[PLATFORM]-[TYPE]-[NN] for templates; okwe-knowledge-[series]-[topic]-slide-NN.png for exports.
  • Files live in the structure below; nothing important lives only in a chat thread.
OKWE KNOWLEDGE
├── 01 BRAND            logo, colour, type, guidelines
├── 02 DESIGN SYSTEM    tokens, components, templates
├── 03 SOCIAL           per-platform profile assets + scheduled assets
├── 04 CONTENT          00 questions · 01 research · 02 drafts · 03 published · 04 archive
├── 05 TEMPLATES        source files, versioned
├── 06 ACADEMY          workshops, courses, workbooks
├── 07 RESEARCH         datasets, method notes, interview logs
└── 08 ANALYTICS        weekly numbers, experiments, learning notes

Two additions to the brief's structure: 04/00 questions (the register is upstream of everything) and 08 learning notes (measurement without a written conclusion is decoration).

Tooling recommendation

  • Brand source of truth: this design system (tokens + components).
  • Social production: the Okwe Post Editor for branded assets; Canva only for one-off internal material.
  • Video: any NLE; title cards and lower thirds exported from the Post Editor at slide size.
  • Presentation: HTML deck built on these tokens, exported to PDF/PPTX.
  • Documentation: plain Markdown in the repo. No tool lock-in.

title: Visual thesis
heading: The Okwe visual thesis
html:
The Okwe visual thesis

This document is the argument. It records what was wrong with the first system, the five territories tested, the palette and typography candidates, the tests each had to pass, and the decisions that followed.

1. Critique of version one — where it was generic

DecisionWhy it failed
#F4F1EA / #FBFAF6 bone groundA warm off-white is the default ground of every 2020s editorial brand and every AI-generated "premium" identity. It signals taste, not Okwe.
#C8442A persimmon signatureContemporary terracotta. Shared with hundreds of DTC, media and edtech brands. Arrived at by mood, not by meaning.
Newsreader + Public SansThe "elegant serif for intelligence + clean sans for clarity" formula. Competent, and completely non-identifying.
3px-radius cards with hover shadowsWeb-app convention imported wholesale. Cards are containers; containers are not an identity.
Pill-shaped tags, soft --shadow-1/2/3 ladderTrend defaults. They exist in every design system of the last decade.
The dot row as brand markThe concept (okwe counters) was right; v2 initially over-corrected and dropped it entirely.
12-column grid, centred hero, generous whitespaceThe layout said "modern site", not "knowledge institution".
Logo-removal testFailed. With the wordmark covered, nothing identified the page.
50-brands testFailed. Palette, type pairing and layout could transfer unchanged to fifty consulting, edtech or media brands.
AI-generation testFailed. It looked like the answer to the prompt "premium modern African knowledge platform".

The diagnosis: version one branded the container. Okwe's actual product is structured information — decompositions, measurements, evidence with stated limits. The identity had to live in how information is notated, not in the colour of the page.

2. Five territories

A — Knowledge Infrastructure (indexing, archives, notation, technical drawing)

Concept: the brand as a catalogue. Every asset carries a call number; diagrams read as technical plans. Emotional effect: authority through order. You trust it because it is filed. Type: mono + expanded grotesk. Colour: single-ink blueprint. Graphic language: rules, indices, plates. Advantage: ownable, cheap to produce (one ink), and it gets stronger as the archive grows — perfect for a brand that will publish 1,000 pieces. Disadvantage: risks looking like a software dashboard if the mono is over-used.

B — Economic Systems (flows, nodes, exchange, movement)

Concept: the brand as a network map. Emotional effect: dynamism, connection. Advantage: matches the ecosystem story (Knowledge → Commerce → Movement). Disadvantage: node-and-edge graphics are the visual language of every fintech and logistics startup on earth; arrows are the most exhausted device in business design. Rejected as a primary territory, kept as an input to the manifest diagram (which deliberately removes arrows).

C — Institutional Modernism (a 21st-century institution founded today)

Concept: the seal, the register, the annual report — but new. Emotional effect: permanence. Advantage: credibility in Lagos, London and Singapore alike. Disadvantage: slides towards ministry or university if it takes on crests, gold or centred symmetry; and permanence can read as stasis for a brand that has published nothing yet.

D — Intellectual Publishing (research culture, serious long-form)

Concept: the journal, the working paper. Emotional effect: rigour. Advantage: the reading experience is the product. Disadvantage: the visual conventions (serif masthead, thin rules, drop caps) are exactly what version one already did, and what every think tank does.

E — Okwe as a native language (the most experimental)

Concept: start from okwe itself — a board of pits where seeds are counted, moved, and compounded — and from the material culture of the economy Okwe writes about: waybills, manifests, tally books, customs stamps, triplicate forms. Emotional effect: this was made by people who actually count things. Advantage: unavailable to any competitor, because it comes from the name and the subject rather than from a category. Disadvantage: could turn nostalgic if it imitates old paperwork instead of abstracting it.

The synthesis (what was built)

A + E, disciplined by C. The brand is a working document of the real economy: a catalogued, notated, counted register — drawn in blueprint ink on mineral ground, with sulphur as the marking ink. D supplies the reading typography; B survives only inside the arrow-free manifest diagram.

3. Three palette candidates

Each candidate was tested against: what it communicates · why it belongs to Okwe · who already owns it · which territory it places Okwe in · ownability · digital behaviour · print behaviour · international read · survival without the logo.

Palette A — Conservative: "Register" (graphite + oxblood + ledger grey)

#1C1E1D graphite · #E8E9E5 grey paper · #6E2A22 oxblood · #3F4A44 slate green

  • Communicates: archive, permanence, seriousness. Belongs: ledger and stamp culture.
  • Already owned by: law firms, heritage publishers, luxury stationery. Oxblood is the "premium" default of the last five years.
  • Accessibility: excellent (14:1 body). Print: two spot inks. International: reads formal everywhere.
  • Without the logo: weak — graphite-on-grey is the safest system in existence.
  • Verdict: credible and forgettable. It passes the institution test and fails the 50-brands test.

Palette B — Distinctive: "Cyanotype" (chalk + cyanotype + sulphur + verdigris + stamp) ★ recommended

#E6EAE7 chalk · #05161F cyanotype · #E3CB2A sulphur · #1E6E63 verdigris · #A8202C stamp

  • Communicates: the technical drawing of a system, annotated by someone who measured it. Cool, precise, materially specific.
  • Belongs to Okwe because: the cyanotype is the drawing that explains how a thing works — Okwe's entire editorial promise. Sulphur is a traded bulk commodity, the ferric chemistry of the blueprint itself, and the colour of an annotation. Verdigris is oxidised copper: the metal that wires an economy, changed by exposure — knowledge from experience. Stamp red is the ink of paperwork authority. Every colour is a material in the economy Okwe writes about, not a mood.
  • Already owned by: blueprint blue appears in some architecture and engineering brands; nobody in education, business media or knowledge platforms owns cyanotype + sulphur. Sulphur yellow is almost unused at brand level outside of hazard signage — and never with a cool blue-green ground.
  • Territory: knowledge infrastructure — exactly where Okwe wants to sit.
  • Digital: cyanotype-800 on chalk-100 = 13.9:1; sulphur is deliberately restricted to marks, rules, tallies and one control, where its low contrast against chalk is irrelevant. Plate mode inverts to a real second mode, not a comfort setting.
  • Print: two inks cover 90% of assets (cyanotype + sulphur); a mono report can print in one. Cheap, which matters at zero budget. Sulphur is achievable in CMYK (≈ 0/8/92/6) and as PMS 604/605.
  • International: blue-green reads technical and neutral in every market; the yellow reads as marking, not as gold.
  • Without the logo: strong — the chalk/cyanotype/sulphur triad plus mono notation is identifiable at thumbnail scale.

Palette C — Experimental: "Cargo" (bitumen black + tarpaulin blue + high-vis)

#14100E bitumen · #0B4FA0 tarpaulin blue · #D8FF3E high-vis · #F2EFE9 sack

  • Communicates: ports, freight, the physical economy at its loudest.
  • Belongs: viscerally to movement and trade.
  • Already owned by: streetwear, sneaker and crypto brands; acid lime is the most fashionable colour of the mid-2020s, which fails the ten-years test on its own.
  • Print: high-vis is unprintable in CMYK without a fifth ink.
  • Verdict: memorable and wrong. It reads as a hype brand, not as a knowledge institution, and it would date by 2028.

Recommendation: Palette B. It is the only candidate where each colour has a material reason to exist, where the system survives the logo-removal test, and where the production cost stays inside a two-person budget.

4. Three typographic candidates

Tested against: why this face · what its geometry says · what it says about Okwe · difference from the sector default · long-form · data · social · presentation · web · weights · licensing · longevity.

Typography A — Institutional: Source Serif 4 + Source Sans 3 + Source Code Pro

  • Geometry: humanist, transparent, Adobe-commissioned for institutions.
  • Long-form: excellent. Data: good tabular figures. Licensing: OFL, permanent.
  • Difference from sector default: minimal — this is the "trustworthy institution" stack, and it is invisible by design.
  • Verdict: faultless and anonymous. Fails the logo-removal test at the type level.

Typography B — Distinctive: Archivo (variable width) + Literata + Martian Mono ★ recommended

  • Archivo: a signage/documentary grotesk with a width axis from 62.5% to 125%. Okwe sets headlines at 118–125%, so a headline arrives as a stamped block of text rather than a fashionable neo-grotesk line. This is a behaviour no competitor can copy without copying the behaviour, not the font.
  • Literata: a sturdy, low-contrast reading serif built for screens. Institutional without being decorative; nothing like Playfair or Cormorant.
  • Martian Mono: squarish mono with unusually strong, wide numerals — set at 87.5% width with 0.14em tracking for every call number, label and figure. Okwe's numbers are its evidence, so the numerals had to be the most distinctive letterforms in the system.
  • The owned move — WIDTH CONTRAST: narrow tracked mono sitting directly above extremely expanded display type. Recognisable at 210px thumbnail size, before colour registers.
  • Long-form: Literata. Data: Martian Mono, tabular. Social: Archivo expanded survives phone-scale. Presentation: the same three faces at register sizes. Weights: 400–800 plus italics and two variable axes. Licensing: all three OFL on Google Fonts — practical for a two-person team, unlikely to disappear.
  • Verdict: distinctive through behaviour rather than novelty, which is what survives ten years.

Typography C — Experimental: Redaction + Anybody + Courier Prime

  • Geometry: deliberately degraded/halftone display, extreme-width variable sans, typewriter mono.
  • Character: unmistakable, and unmistakably a design-industry gesture. Redaction's halftone breaks up at small sizes; Courier Prime is weak for UI and terrible for data density.
  • Verdict: rejected. It performs authorship instead of supporting information.

Recommendation: Typography B.

6. The thesis

Okwe should look like the working document of the real economy: a catalogued, annotated, counted register — drawn in blueprint ink on mineral ground, marked in sulphur where something matters. The identity lives in how information is notated, not in the shape of a container, so it strengthens as Okwe publishes rather than dating. Remove the wordmark and the call number, the expanded headline against narrow mono, the tally and the margin note still say Okwe.

Colour thesis. Five materials with reasons: chalk (mineral ground, never cream), cyanotype (the blueprint ink), sulphur (commodity, chemistry, annotation — marks and counts, never fills), verdigris (oxidised copper: systems and second data series), stamp red (paperwork authority, rationed to corrections and opinion). One accent per surface. Plate mode is a second printing plate, not a comfort mode.

Typography thesis. Three faces, three jobs, one behaviour: width contrast. Archivo at 118–125% for statements, Martian Mono at 87.5% with wide tracking for the register, Literata for reading. Numbers are always tabular mono and usually oversized — Okwe's evidence deserves the biggest type on the page.

Layout thesis. The ledger: a 104px index rail, a 640px reading field, a 216px annotation margin. Rules that run edge to edge, never boxes. Zero radii — every radius token resolves to 0px so a stray corner cannot enter through a token. No elevation system: separation comes from rules and ground. Asymmetric, hung left, dense against sparse.

Information-design thesis. This is the differentiator. Four devices: the call number (everything is catalogued), the tally (proportions are counted in sulphur squares, from okwe's seeds), the manifest diagram (stages on one ruled baseline with square joints — no arrows, no nodes), and the margin note (sources, method and stated gaps hang beside the claim). An Okwe diagram is recognisable with every colour stripped out.

Photography thesis. Documentary field images of real operations — terminals, warehouses, workshops, paperwork, hands, machinery — shot cool, mid-contrast, unfiltered, square-cornered, and always captioned in mono with place and date. Archive and cover images take the cyanotype plate treatment (single ink). Type sits over photography only as display type over the protection plate. No illustration, no stock optimism, no orange-and-teal grade.

Graphic-language thesis. Five recurring devices, each conceptually tied to knowledge, systems or measurement: call number, tally, manifest, margin note, and the class stamp (fact / our reading / our view / unresolved). Nothing decorative is permitted to recur.

Motion thesis. Mechanical: 90ms snap on controls, 140ms on panels, 200ms for a dialog frame landing, and stepped counting (steps(10,end)) for tallies — the only "expressive" motion in the system, and it expresses arithmetic. No bounce, no spring, no scale-in, no parallax.

Social-content thesis. Every canvas is the same ledger sheet at platform size: index band (call number, series, class stamp, date) · content field · register foot (wordmark, tally, destination). Cover parts take the cyanotype plate, comparisons verdigris, the closing part sulphur, everything else chalk. A statistic cannot render without a source line. The set reads as one document, and any single part read alone still says where it came from.

8. Test results, version two

  • No-logo test: pass. See guidelines/cards/brand-nologo.html and the twelve proofs in ui_kits/content_proofs/.
  • 50-brands test: the palette, the width behaviour, the tally and the manifest cannot transfer without transferring the concept.
  • AI-generation test: the system contains no warm neutral, no terracotta, no serif/sans "elegance" pairing, no rounded cards, no gradients, no soft shadows.
  • Ten-years test: two variable open-licence families, one accent restricted by rule, an identity that grows with the archive.
  • Institution test: report, workshop cover, thumbnail, carousel, presentation and data card built from the same three bands — see the proofs.
  • Premium-cliché test: no gold, no serif small caps, no marble, no letterpress texture. Valuable, not luxurious.
